Principaux résultats
  * Déploiement mondial sur trois mois grâce à un partenariat étroit avec l'équipe des services professionnels d'Algolia
  * Fort impact commercial à l'échelle mondiale, avec notamment une hausse de 33 % des conversions aux États-Unis et de 175 % en Corée. 
  * Amélioration de 81 % du temps de réponse PLP, améliorant considérablement l'expérience utilisateur
  * Commercialisation simplifiée sur plusieurs marchés


## Découvrez Crocs
Leader mondial des chaussures décontractées innovantes, Crocs propose certes des chaussures confortables et amortissantes, mais sa domination sur le marché de la chaussure est tout sauf timide.
Partie de ses modestes débuts dans le développement d'une chaussure bateau en mousse devenue emblématique, cette entreprise basée au Colorado est devenue une puissance internationale présente dans le monde entier et possédant de multiples marques, offrant tout, des sandales aux baskets en passant par les bottes d'hiver avec des options de personnalisation.
Aujourd'hui, Crocs propose une gamme variée de modèles pour hommes, femmes et enfants, avec des collections et des coloris distincts pour s'adapter à toutes les occasions et à toutes les saisons. Offrir confort, innovation et plaisir aux pieds du monde entier est plus complexe qu'il n'y paraît, et l'entreprise s'efforce de créer une expérience d'achat fluide, cohérente et agréable pour ses millions de clients.
## **Défi : intensifier la recherche à l'échelle mondiale**
  * Optimisation de la recherche à l'échelle mondiale pour plusieurs marques et régions
  * Gérer un catalogue vaste et diversifié tout en veillant à ce que le bon produit soit mis en avant au bon moment.
  * Le manque de transparence concernant la logique de recherche de l'IA rend difficile l'optimisation de la pertinence.
  * La charge de travail manuelle importante liée au merchandising réduit la concentration sur d'autres tâches à plus forte valeur ajoutée.


Pour aider une clientèle aussi diversifiée, répartie sur des dizaines de régions et proposant de nombreuses références, à trouver exactement ce qu'elle recherche, il faut une recherche pertinente, rapide et fluide, afin que les clients ne disent pas « à plus tard » avant même d'avoir commencé.
Avec deux marques, un catalogue important et dynamique, des sites régionaux et plusieurs équipes de merchandising pour les gérer, s'adapter aux comportements d'achat modernes représentait un véritable défi. Le manque de constance dans la pertinence des offres et le manque de transparence ont rendu la mise en avant des bons produits au bon moment particulièrement complexe.
Le manque de transparence de Crocs concernant la logique d'IA utilisée par leur solution existante ne permettait pas de comprendre pourquoi les résultats s'affichaient de cette manière, ce qui rendait difficile de déterminer si elle était réellement utile. 
« Notre système actuel exigeait un travail manuel considérable pour atteindre nos objectifs », explique Feliz Papich. « Compte tenu de la taille et de la diversité de notre catalogue, il n’est pas envisageable de gérer individuellement chaque produit. »
« Nous savions que nous pouvions faire davantage avec la recherche pour améliorer la pertinence et l'expérience client globale, mais pour y parvenir, nous avions besoin d'une solution capable de gérer l'envergure de notre catalogue et la portée de nos opérations. »
## Solution : Une mise à niveau globale de la recherche sans faille
  * Migration vers Algolia comme base pour la recherche et la navigation
  * Un studio de merchandising pour réduire la charge de travail manuelle des équipes commerciales régionales
  * Formation et collaboration mondiales entre Algolia et Crocs, malgré les décalages horaires.
  * Réorganisation dynamique pour automatiser et améliorer la pertinence en fonction du comportement des utilisateurs


Une évaluation précédente d'Algolia par HEYDUDE avait permis à l'équipe Crocs de se familiariser avec la solution, sa flexibilité, son évolutivité, ses performances et sa vision de l'IA. Impressionnée par les récentes améliorations apportées à Merchandising Studio, elle a pris contact avec Algolia.
« Le studio de merchandising convivial d'Algolia a été un atout majeur, offrant aux équipes de merchandising régionales une meilleure visibilité, un contrôle accru et la possibilité de configurer facilement l'expérience d'achat en ligne », explique Feliz.
Crocs a déployé Algolia pour la recherche, la navigation et la saisie semi-automatique sur ses deux marques et dans plus d'une douzaine de régions et de sites à travers le monde. L'équipe a également mis en œuvre le reclassement dynamique (DRR) afin d'améliorer la pertinence des résultats en fonction du comportement des clients.
Crocs prévoyait initialement de déployer Algolia uniquement pour la recherche, mais a rapidement étendu son périmètre pour inclure la navigation dans le cadre du lancement. Avec un délai ambitieux de trois mois pour un déploiement mondial et un besoin d'homogénéité entre les régions, Crocs a collaboré étroitement avec l'équipe des services professionnels d'Algolia (solutions clients, stratégie commerciale et intégrations).
Lors de la mise en œuvre, Algolia a accompagné Crocs dans la migration des données, l'optimisation de la pertinence et la préparation du merchandising. Des formations ont été dispensées aux équipes merchandising d'Amérique du Nord, d'Europe et d'Asie-Pacifique afin de garantir leur maîtrise d'Algolia et de Merchandising Studio. 
Grâce à ce solide partenariat interfonctionnel et aux résultats obtenus dès le lancement, Crocs était bien placé pour étendre son utilisation d'Algolia et explorer des fonctionnalités plus avancées au fil du temps.
## Résultats : Des gains immédiats à l'adoption avancée de l'IA
  * Réduction de 81 % du temps de réponse PLP
  * Amélioration des taux de conversion dans plusieurs régions, notamment une hausse de 33 % aux États-Unis grâce à InstantSearch et une augmentation de 175 % des conversions de navigation en Corée.
  * Augmentation des taux de clics, amélioration du positionnement dans les résultats de recherche et hausse des taux d'ajout au panier et d'achat grâce au reclassement dynamique.


Trente jours seulement après son lancement, Crocs a constaté un impact mondial grâce à sa nouvelle expérience de recherche et de découverte optimisée par Algolia, générant des gains sur des marchés clés.
Les améliorations des taux de conversion ont été constantes pour toutes les expériences. InstantSearch a généré des hausses notables, avec des gains de 33 %, 42 % et 79 % respectivement aux États-Unis, au Canada et en Australie. Browse a également joué un rôle crucial, avec une augmentation des conversions de plus de 175 % en Corée, tandis que des marchés comme l'Allemagne et l'Australie ont enregistré de fortes améliorations des taux de conversion de la recherche principale, allant d'une vingtaine à une quarantaine de pour cent.
Parallèlement, les améliorations de performance ont considérablement optimisé l'expérience utilisateur. Crocs a ainsi réduit de 81 % les temps de réponse des applications de suivi des achats (PLP), permettant des parcours d'achat plus rapides et plus fluides, ce qui a directement contribué à l'augmentation de l'engagement et des taux de conversion.
Fort de ces premiers résultats prometteurs, Crocs est passé à une phase d'optimisation afin d'améliorer encore ses performances. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle phase, l'équipe a mis en œuvre le Dynamic Re-Ranking (DRR) pour affiner en permanence la pertinence des produits en fonction du comportement des utilisateurs, tout en réduisant considérablement les efforts manuels de merchandising.
Cette initiative a permis d'obtenir des améliorations mesurables sur les indicateurs clés, impactant à la fois le tunnel de conversion et, en fin de compte, le chiffre d'affaires des marques Crocs et HEYDUDE. Les tests A/B ont montré que le marché américain de Crocs, le site le plus visité de l'entreprise, a connu :
  * +2,4 % du taux de clics (CTR)
  * Amélioration de 5,6 % de la position moyenne des clics
  * +2,3 % du taux d'ajout au panier
  * +3,8 % du taux d'achat


S'appuyant sur ces excellents résultats et sur son partenariat étroit avec les équipes d'Algolia, Crocs a rapidement standardisé ses processus sur Algolia dans toutes ses régions et pour toutes ses équipes merchandising, puis a opté pour le plan Elevate afin de bénéficier de fonctionnalités plus avancées. Grâce à Elevate, l'équipe a désormais accès à des fonctionnalités de pointe, telles que NeuralSearch, les collections IA, les groupes intelligents et la personnalisation en temps réel, qu'elle exploite activement pour optimiser la découverte des produits, automatiser le merchandising et proposer des expériences client plus personnalisées à grande échelle.

# Spain won the World Cup. It also won search.
Published:  July 29, 2026
[ Back to all blogs ](https://www.algolia.com/blog/algolia)
Spain won the World Cup. It also won search.
Table of Contents
Get a customized demo from our search experts
[ Get a demo ](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)
Listen to the brief:
Your browser does not support the audio element. 
The final whistle has blown, but the World Cup is still teaching retailers an important lesson: cultural moments can change shopping behavior in an instant.
Across Algolia’s AI Search platform, which powers nearly 2 trillion searches annually for more than 18,000 companies, fans searched for teams, players and merchandise as the tournament unfolded.
## The final weekend, by the numbers
From July 17-19, consumers across the U.S. and Europe generated:
  * 160,000 searches for soccer kits, jerseys, football shirts and related terms
  * 139,000 searches for Spain, compared with 110,000 for Argentina, giving Spain the win in both the final and the “search match”
  * A 93% day-over-day surge in searches for Spanish right winger “Yamal” on July 19 (the day Yamal took home the FIFA World Cup Trophy), reaching over 30,000 searches
  * 461,000 searches for Messi on July 19, showing the enduring pull of an established global star


Though, the search momentum started well beyond the final:
  * During the first two weeks of the tournament, World Cup searches were over 34% higher than the prior two-week period, with over 1.16 million searches across the U.S. and Europe
  * U.S. consumers searched for soccer kits and jerseys an average of more than 31,000 times per day throughout the entire tournament
  * Norwegian striker Haaland became a fan favorite midway through the tournament, generating nearly 7,000 U.S. searches in the week after Norway’s quarterfinal loss


The numbers show how quickly attention can turn into product discovery. Here are four lessons for retailers preparing for the next major sporting moment.
## 1. Demand can spike without warning
Search behavior rose around specific matches, players and cultural moments rather than following a predictable path.
Retailers cannot anticipate every breakout star or viral play. They can ensure their search infrastructure is ready when one arrives. Strong uptime, fast results and the ability to withstand sudden traffic peaks are essential when shoppers are acting in real time.
## 2. Shoppers rarely use the same words
One fan may search for a “football shirt.” Another may type “soccer kit,” “Spain jersey” or simply a player’s name.
AI-powered search must understand the intent connecting those phrases, including regional language, product attributes and context. Exact keyword matching is not enough when shoppers across markets are looking for the same product in different ways.
## 3. Limited-time products need instant visibility
Championship apparel, player merchandise and commemorative products have short selling windows.
Retailers need to:
  * Elevate relevant products quickly
  * Incorporate real-time demand signals
  * Make new releases searchable as soon as they become available
  * Personalize results by team, player, size and style


If merchandise is buried, poorly categorized or slow to appear, the moment may pass before shoppers find it.
## 4. Discovery extends beyond a retailer’s website
A fan may ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Claude where to buy a Spain jersey before visiting a retailer directly.
Product data must therefore be accurate, structured and accessible wherever discovery begins. A reliable search and retrieval layer can help retailers surface relevant products both on their own sites and through external AI-powered shopping tools.
## The next spike is already approaching
The World Cup may be over, but the U.S. Open and American football season are approaching. LA28 will be here in the blink of an eye.
Each event will produce unexpected stars, viral moments and limited-time demand. Retailers do not need to know exactly what shoppers will search for. They need an AI strategy that can:
  * Understand intent across different search terms
  * Maintain performance during traffic peaks
  * Surface timely merchandise immediately
  * Support discovery across websites and AI tools


Moments move quickly. Retail search needs to move faster.
To learn how Algolia helps retailers deliver fast and intuitive search, generative, and agentic experiences during major sports moments,[ connect with our team for a demo.](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)

# Hallucination mitigation in enterprise search
Published:  August 04, 2026
[ Back to all blogs ](https://www.algolia.com/blog/ai)
Hallucination mitigation in enterprise search
Table of Contents
Get a customized demo from our search experts
[ Get a demo ](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)
Listen to the brief:
Your browser does not support the audio element. 
When an enterprise search system invents an answer, the damage rarely stays on the screen. A fabricated troubleshooting step sends a support agent down the wrong path and opens more tickets. A wrong figure about an approval threshold pushes a finance decision the wrong way. In legal and compliance work, an unsupported answer can look authoritative enough to be used before anyone checks it. In healthcare and other regulated settings, stale guidance carries immediate risk. Internal knowledge search has the same shape, since employees route issues, resolve incidents, and interpret policy from whatever the search box returns.
A wrong answer costs something when a person acts on it. In agentic workflows, the answer can trigger an API call, an escalation, a refund, a status change, or a customer message before anyone reviews it. Engineering leaders treat hallucination as a production blocker because risk grows with the action attached to the answer. We go further in depth on this subject in our white paper, [Hallucination Mitigation in Enterprise Search](https://www.algolia.com/resources/asset/white-paper-hallucination-mitigation-in-enterprise-search), but here are the highlights.
## Prompting is not the fix
The instinct is to fix hallucination with a better prompt. The prompt can tell the model to use provided sources and refuse when evidence is weak. It reduces visible errors. Production reliability comes from retrieval and runtime controls. Before generation begins, the retrieval path returns approved material, keeps it current, and applies user scope. The enterprise problem starts earlier in the pipeline and continues past generation, so the control logic needs to run across the whole response path.
The production path needs grounded retrieval, answerability detection, citation and verifiability enforcement, and [policy guardrails](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf) working together. They decide what reaches generation, when the system should stop, how claims remain checkable, and what can be released.
## Grounded retrieval
Retrieval is the first line of defense because the model cannot answer better than the evidence it receives. Wrong, stale, or out-of-scope passages put generation into a compromised state, and a fluent answer built on weak evidence still reads as confident.
Enterprise retrieval has two common failure modes. Keyword search misses paraphrase and concept-level matches when users phrase a request in their own words. Vector search returns semantically related material and can drift past the exact policy term, product name, or contract clause needed to support the answer.             "hitsPerPage": k_final,
        },
    )

    return response.hits

Grounding ties an answer to retrieved evidence. Answerability checks if the support is strong enough to answer. When support falls below threshold, the response path changes by workflow. The system abstains or returns a narrower answer. A source link shows where the system searched. Claim-level attribution shows the passage, field, or record behind each statement. Policy, pricing, contract, and procedure work need claim-level support.

Citation quality carries as much weight as citation presence. A loose citation leaves the reviewer to rebuild the support path.
## Policy guardrails
Access and release boundaries create another failure path. A correct answer is unsafe when it uses a document outside the user’s permissions, follows hostile instructions from retrieved content, or exposes regulated data. Control failures need enforcement on both sides of generation.

Output-side controls run before release. PII suppression, unsafe-content filtering, redaction, and response validation check the answer against access and policy rules. Each blocked query, filtered result, and redacted span leaves an audit signal. Risk and compliance teams need a record of why an answer was returned, narrowed, or stopped.
## Why these controls belong in the search layer
Filtering, ranking, permission enforcement, and orchestration belong in the retrieval and serving path. They run at query time, inside production latency budgets. When teams rebuild the same logic in application code, ranking, access, and index coordination start changing separately. Under latency pressure, teams remove the checks that catch unsupported answers.
A raw vector store returns semantically similar records. Enterprise AI search needs more than similarity. Multi-index orchestration, ACL-aware retrieval, runtime filtering, and permission-scoped serving need to work before generation.     },

# Spain won the World Cup. It also won search.
Published:  July 29, 2026
[ Back to all blogs ](https://www.algolia.com/blog/algolia)
Spain won the World Cup. It also won search.
Table of Contents
Get a customized demo from our search experts
[ Get a demo ](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)
Listen to the brief:
Your browser does not support the audio element. 
The final whistle has blown, but the World Cup is still teaching retailers an important lesson: cultural moments can change shopping behavior in an instant.
Across Algolia’s AI Search platform, which powers nearly 2 trillion searches annually for more than 18,000 companies, fans searched for teams, players and merchandise as the tournament unfolded.
## The final weekend, by the numbers
From July 17-19, consumers across the U.S. and Europe generated:
  * 160,000 searches for soccer kits, jerseys, football shirts and related terms
  * 139,000 searches for Spain, compared with 110,000 for Argentina, giving Spain the win in both the final and the “search match”
  * A 93% day-over-day surge in searches for Spanish right winger “Yamal” on July 19 (the day Yamal took home the FIFA World Cup Trophy), reaching over 30,000 searches
  * 461,000 searches for Messi on July 19, showing the enduring pull of an established global star


Though, the search momentum started well beyond the final:
  * During the first two weeks of the tournament, World Cup searches were over 34% higher than the prior two-week period, with over 1.16 million searches across the U.S. and Europe
  * U.S. consumers searched for soccer kits and jerseys an average of more than 31,000 times per day throughout the entire tournament
  * Norwegian striker Haaland became a fan favorite midway through the tournament, generating nearly 7,000 U.S. searches in the week after Norway’s quarterfinal loss


The numbers show how quickly attention can turn into product discovery. Here are four lessons for retailers preparing for the next major sporting moment.
## 1. Demand can spike without warning
Search behavior rose around specific matches, players and cultural moments rather than following a predictable path.
Retailers cannot anticipate every breakout star or viral play. They can ensure their search infrastructure is ready when one arrives. Strong uptime, fast results and the ability to withstand sudden traffic peaks are essential when shoppers are acting in real time.
## 2. Shoppers rarely use the same words
One fan may search for a “football shirt.” Another may type “soccer kit,” “Spain jersey” or simply a player’s name.
AI-powered search must understand the intent connecting those phrases, including regional language, product attributes and context. Exact keyword matching is not enough when shoppers across markets are looking for the same product in different ways.
## 3. Limited-time products need instant visibility
Championship apparel, player merchandise and commemorative products have short selling windows.
Retailers need to:
  * Elevate relevant products quickly
  * Incorporate real-time demand signals
  * Make new releases searchable as soon as they become available
  * Personalize results by team, player, size and style


If merchandise is buried, poorly categorized or slow to appear, the moment may pass before shoppers find it.
## 4. Discovery extends beyond a retailer’s website
A fan may ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Claude where to buy a Spain jersey before visiting a retailer directly.
Product data must therefore be accurate, structured and accessible wherever discovery begins. A reliable search and retrieval layer can help retailers surface relevant products both on their own sites and through external AI-powered shopping tools.
## The next spike is already approaching
The World Cup may be over, but the U.S. Open and American football season are approaching. LA28 will be here in the blink of an eye.
Each event will produce unexpected stars, viral moments and limited-time demand. Retailers do not need to know exactly what shoppers will search for. They need an AI strategy that can:
  * Understand intent across different search terms
  * Maintain performance during traffic peaks
  * Surface timely merchandise immediately
  * Support discovery across websites and AI tools


Moments move quickly. Retail search needs to move faster.
To learn how Algolia helps retailers deliver fast and intuitive search, generative, and agentic experiences during major sports moments,[ connect with our team for a demo.](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)

# Hallucination mitigation in enterprise search
Published:  August 04, 2026
[ Back to all blogs ](https://www.algolia.com/blog/ai)
Hallucination mitigation in enterprise search
Table of Contents
Get a customized demo from our search experts
[ Get a demo ](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)
Listen to the brief:
Your browser does not support the audio element. 
When an enterprise search system invents an answer, the damage rarely stays on the screen. A fabricated troubleshooting step sends a support agent down the wrong path and opens more tickets. A wrong figure about an approval threshold pushes a finance decision the wrong way. In legal and compliance work, an unsupported answer can look authoritative enough to be used before anyone checks it. In healthcare and other regulated settings, stale guidance carries immediate risk. Internal knowledge search has the same shape, since employees route issues, resolve incidents, and interpret policy from whatever the search box returns.
A wrong answer costs something when a person acts on it. In agentic workflows, the answer can trigger an API call, an escalation, a refund, a status change, or a customer message before anyone reviews it. Engineering leaders treat hallucination as a production blocker because risk grows with the action attached to the answer. We go further in depth on this subject in our white paper, [Hallucination Mitigation in Enterprise Search](https://www.algolia.com/resources/asset/white-paper-hallucination-mitigation-in-enterprise-search), but here are the highlights.
## Prompting is not the fix
The instinct is to fix hallucination with a better prompt. The prompt can tell the model to use provided sources and refuse when evidence is weak. It reduces visible errors. Production reliability comes from retrieval and runtime controls. Before generation begins, the retrieval path returns approved material, keeps it current, and applies user scope. The enterprise problem starts earlier in the pipeline and continues past generation, so the control logic needs to run across the whole response path.
The production path needs grounded retrieval, answerability detection, citation and verifiability enforcement, and [policy guardrails](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf) working together. They decide what reaches generation, when the system should stop, how claims remain checkable, and what can be released.
## Grounded retrieval
Retrieval is the first line of defense because the model cannot answer better than the evidence it receives. Wrong, stale, or out-of-scope passages put generation into a compromised state, and a fluent answer built on weak evidence still reads as confident.
Enterprise retrieval has two common failure modes. Keyword search misses paraphrase and concept-level matches when users phrase a request in their own words. Vector search returns semantically related material and can drift past the exact policy term, product name, or contract clause needed to support the answer. Hybrid retrieval reduces both errors by combining lexical precision with semantic reach, then ranking the merged set. Reranking turns a broad candidate pool into a usable evidence set. It promotes passages with direct support and demotes passages with only topic language. Metadata filtering applies access, region, document type, and freshness constraints before generation, which keeps a draft policy or the wrong regional rule out of the evidence set. Chunking keeps qualifiers and exceptions attached to the passages they change. Poor chunking separates context and weakens the evidence.
Here is a scoped retrieval call in the current Algolia Search 4.x Python client style.

```
from algoliasearch.search.client import SearchClientSync

client = SearchClientSync("YOUR_APP_ID", "YOUR_SEARCH_API_KEY")

def retrieve_evidence(query, user_scope, k_final=8):
    # Assume the target index is configured for Algolia NeuralSearch.
    # user_scope.facet_filters is supplied by the application's access-control layer.
    response = client.search_single_index(
        index_name="enterprise_docs",
        search_params={
            "query": query,
            "filters": "policy_state:approved AND is_current:true",
            "facetFilters": user_scope.facet_filters,
            "hitsPerPage": k_final,
        },
    )

    return response.hits
```

The filters carry policy state and freshness. The facet filters carry user scope. The evidence set reaching the model is already narrowed to what is approved, current, and visible to the person asking. This example assumes the index, searchable attributes, filterable attributes, NeuralSearch configuration, and user-scope filters already exist. Enforced user-restricted access is handled separately with secured API keys.
## Answerability detection
Grounding ties an answer to retrieved evidence. Answerability checks if the support is strong enough to answer. Retrieved passages can be real, current, and policy-safe and still fall short of the actual question. [Answerability detection](https://aclanthology.org/2025.tacl-1.26/) keeps partial matches, conflicting sources, and single-branch support from entering generation as enough evidence. Without it, the model produces a confident answer regardless of the support.
Answerability uses several signals. Coverage checks show whether the evidence spans the whole question or only part of it. Support validation tests whether a passage actually backs the proposed claim or only shares vocabulary with it. A verifier model can inspect a draft answer against the evidence set and flag unsupported spans. A classifier gate can catch clear no-answer cases before generation runs. A confidence score is useful when it reflects support quality.
When support falls below threshold, the response path changes by workflow. The system abstains or returns a narrower answer. A narrower answer covers the supported branch and marks the rest as unsupported. In regulated or high-risk work, the answer path stops for human review. Higher-risk tasks require stronger evidence. A compliance interpretation needs stronger support than a product discovery query. A response that says "I cannot support this from the current sources" is safer than a complete answer built on weak support.
## Citation and verifiability
A source link shows where the system searched. Claim-level attribution shows the passage, field, or record behind each statement. Policy, pricing, contract, and procedure work need claim-level support.
[Attribution starts before final wording is produced](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.182/). The system connects each intended claim to supporting evidence, constrains generation to that support, and checks the final answer against it. Failures become easier to diagnose. A missing citation shows an answer running past its evidence. An overbroad citation means weak chunking or ranking. A wrong document version points to a freshness or metadata problem. Citation quality carries as much weight as citation presence. A loose citation leaves the reviewer to rebuild the support path.
## Policy guardrails
Access and release boundaries create another failure path. A correct answer is unsafe when it uses a document outside the user’s permissions, follows hostile instructions from retrieved content, or exposes regulated data. Control failures need enforcement on both sides of generation.
Input-side controls run before and during retrieval. Query sanitization blocks hostile or malformed requests. Access-aware retrieval applies user permissions. Policy-aware filtering narrows results by role and data class. [Prompt-injection resistance](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/) limits hostile instructions from the query or retrieved documents. Output-side controls run before release. PII suppression, unsafe-content filtering, redaction, and response validation check the answer against access and policy rules. Each blocked query, filtered result, and redacted span leaves an audit signal. Risk and compliance teams need a record of why an answer was returned, narrowed, or stopped.
## Why these controls belong in the search layer
Filtering, ranking, permission enforcement, and orchestration belong in the retrieval and serving path. They run at query time, inside production latency budgets. When teams rebuild the same logic in application code, ranking, access, and index coordination start changing separately. Under latency pressure, teams remove the checks that catch unsupported answers.
A raw vector store returns semantically similar records. Enterprise AI search needs more than similarity. Multi-index orchestration, ACL-aware retrieval, runtime filtering, and permission-scoped serving need to work before generation. [Algolia AI Search](https://www.algolia.com/products/ai-search) brings retrieval, filtering, ranking, and serving into one search path. [NeuralSearch combines keyword and vector retrieval in a single query](https://algolia.com/doc/guides/ai-relevance/neuralsearch/get-started), so ranking reflects lexical precision and semantic similarity together. For user-restricted retrieval, access scope is enforced with [secured API keys](https://algolia.com/doc/guides/security/api-keys/how-to/user-restricted-access-to-data) and a permission attribute such as visible_by configured as filterOnly(visible_by), so retrieval is scoped to records the user can see.

```

from algoliasearch.search.client import SearchClientSync

client = SearchClientSync("YOUR_APP_ID", "YOUR_SEARCH_ONLY_API_KEY")

secured_key = client.generate_secured_api_key(
    parent_api_key="YOUR_SEARCH_ONLY_API_KEY",
    restrictions={
        "filters": "visible_by:user_123",
        "restrict_indices": ["enterprise_docs"],
    },
)

```

The key is generated server-side from a search-only parent key. Every search made with it is scoped to records the user is allowed to see. 
## Evaluate before you deploy
A production-ready system answers from approved data, abstains when support is weak, cites claims at reviewable depth, and enforces policy before release. Without abstention, citation, and scope enforcement, the architecture is not ready for production.
Evaluate your AI search stack against grounded retrieval, answerability, verifiability, and policy enforcement with our white paper, [Hallucination Mitigation in Enterprise Search](https://www.algolia.com/resources/asset/white-paper-hallucination-mitigation-in-enterprise-search).

# Spain won the World Cup. It also won search.
Published:  July 29, 2026
[ Back to all blogs ](https://www.algolia.com/blog/algolia)
Spain won the World Cup. It also won search.
Table of Contents
Get a customized demo from our search experts
[ Get a demo ](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)
Listen to the brief:
Your browser does not support the audio element. 
The final whistle has blown, but the World Cup is still teaching retailers an important lesson: cultural moments can change shopping behavior in an instant.
Across Algolia’s AI Search platform, which powers nearly 2 trillion searches annually for more than 18,000 companies, fans searched for teams, players and merchandise as the tournament unfolded.
## The final weekend, by the numbers
From July 17-19, consumers across the U.S. and Europe generated:
  * 160,000 searches for soccer kits, jerseys, football shirts and related terms
  * 139,000 searches for Spain, compared with 110,000 for Argentina, giving Spain the win in both the final and the “search match”
  * A 93% day-over-day surge in searches for Spanish right winger “Yamal” on July 19 (the day Yamal took home the FIFA World Cup Trophy), reaching over 30,000 searches
  * 461,000 searches for Messi on July 19, showing the enduring pull of an established global star


Though, the search momentum started well beyond the final:
  * During the first two weeks of the tournament, World Cup searches were over 34% higher than the prior two-week period, with over 1.16 million searches across the U.S. and Europe
  * U.S. consumers searched for soccer kits and jerseys an average of more than 31,000 times per day throughout the entire tournament
  * Norwegian striker Haaland became a fan favorite midway through the tournament, generating nearly 7,000 U.S. searches in the week after Norway’s quarterfinal loss


The numbers show how quickly attention can turn into product discovery. Here are four lessons for retailers preparing for the next major sporting moment.
## 1. Demand can spike without warning
Search behavior rose around specific matches, players and cultural moments rather than following a predictable path.
Retailers cannot anticipate every breakout star or viral play. They can ensure their search infrastructure is ready when one arrives. Strong uptime, fast results and the ability to withstand sudden traffic peaks are essential when shoppers are acting in real time.
## 2. Shoppers rarely use the same words
One fan may search for a “football shirt.” Another may type “soccer kit,” “Spain jersey” or simply a player’s name.
AI-powered search must understand the intent connecting those phrases, including regional language, product attributes and context. Exact keyword matching is not enough when shoppers across markets are looking for the same product in different ways.
## 3. Limited-time products need instant visibility
Championship apparel, player merchandise and commemorative products have short selling windows.
Retailers need to:
  * Elevate relevant products quickly
  * Incorporate real-time demand signals
  * Make new releases searchable as soon as they become available
  * Personalize results by team, player, size and style


If merchandise is buried, poorly categorized or slow to appear, the moment may pass before shoppers find it.
## 4. Discovery extends beyond a retailer’s website
A fan may ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Claude where to buy a Spain jersey before visiting a retailer directly.
Product data must therefore be accurate, structured and accessible wherever discovery begins. A reliable search and retrieval layer can help retailers surface relevant products both on their own sites and through external AI-powered shopping tools.
## The next spike is already approaching
The World Cup may be over, but the U.S. Open and American football season are approaching. LA28 will be here in the blink of an eye.
Each event will produce unexpected stars, viral moments and limited-time demand. Retailers do not need to know exactly what shoppers will search for. They need an AI strategy that can:
  * Understand intent across different search terms
  * Maintain performance during traffic peaks
  * Surface timely merchandise immediately
  * Support discovery across websites and AI tools


Moments move quickly. Retail search needs to move faster.
To learn how Algolia helps retailers deliver fast and intuitive search, generative, and agentic experiences during major sports moments,[ connect with our team for a demo.](https://www.algolia.com/demorequest)
